title: Take one coloured pencil out of a tightly packed flat tin
keywords: lever a part up to grasp it
instruction: Take the red pencil out of the tin and lay it on the sketch pad, leaving the other pencils in the tin.
context: Taking a coloured pencil from a packed tin is a familiar school and drawing activity, but the narrow spacing prevents a direct pinch. This tests making the pencil graspable using its own gravity lever, unlike a book that stays tipped out of a shelf (TK-E6ECW7) or ordinary marker packing (TK-M49TV4).
setup: Positions in mm from the midpoint between the arm bases (x forward, y left, z up from the table). One fixed layout, as in the screenshot. Tin: Tombow CB-NQ12C tin of 12 coloured pencils, painted tinplate, 186 x 102 x 12 mm closed, lying open and loose on the table, 91 g empty (the listed 157 g less its pencils). Its base (184.6 x 100.6 x 10 mm outside, estimated: it fits inside the lid) is centred x 300, y 0, long side along y; its lid (186 x 102 x 7 mm, depth estimated) lies open flat on the far side, centred x 403, joined by its two wire hinges. Pencils: the set's twelve, round, 7.5 mm across and 176 mm long with an 11 mm sharpened cone, 5.5 g each (all four estimated), lying side by side on the base's bare floor, 0.7 mm apart, points to the robot's left (y 87, 4.5 mm from the end wall), blunt ends at y -89; from the near wall to the far one: brown, black, light orange, light blue, green, yellow green, yellow, orange, pink, RED (x 329), purple, blue. Sketch pad: A5, 148 (x) x 210 (y) x 6 mm, white top sheet, taped down, centred x 300, y -235. Both arms start at the ready pose, grippers open. Real-trial cost: about 15 USD for the tin of pencils and a few for the pad; nothing is built.
scoring: Judged at the end of the run; every level counts only with both grippers at least 3 cm from the red pencil. Each level is stated for the simulator and for a real trial (tools: a steel rule, two 2 mm spacers, the final photograph and the last second of video). 1.0: Simulator: the red pencil lies on the sketch pad (all of its length over the pad, within 10 degrees of level, its underside within 3 mm of the pad's top), each of the other eleven lies in the tin's base (both ends inside the base's walls, no part more than 2 mm above the walls' rim), and for 1 s (20 steps) both grippers have stayed 3 cm from the red pencil and no pencil's ends and none of the base's corners has moved more than 1 mm. Real trial: in the final photograph the red pencil lies flat on the pad inside its outline (its two ends' heights differ by under 30 mm on the rule, which is 10 degrees over its 176 mm); a steel rule laid across the base's rim on two 2 mm spacers clears all eleven others; the grippers are 3 cm or more from the red pencil (rule against the photo); and there is no visible motion of the pencils or the tin in the last second of video. 0.75: Simulator: the same, but not yet for 1 s. Real trial: the same photograph checks, with motion visible in the last second or the hand leaving less than 1 s before the end. 0.5: Simulator: released and everything still for 1 s, no part of the red pencil's length over the tin (base or lid), not lying on the pad as above, the other eleven in the base. Real trial: the red pencil lies clear of the tin's outline, base and lid, but not flat inside the pad's outline; the rule-and-spacers check clears the other eleven; no visible motion in the last second. 0.25: Simulator: at rest as for 0.5, the red pencil out of the tin, and one or two of the others not lying in the base (taken out too, lying across the row, propped on a wall). Real trial: the red pencil clear of the tin's outline, and the rule on its spacers touches one or two of the others or they lie outside the base. 0: Simulator: any part of the red pencil's length still over the tin, three or more of the others not lying in the base, or a gripper within 3 cm of the red pencil. Real trial: the red pencil over the tin's outline in the final photograph, three or more others out of place, or the red pencil still held. 0 for good: Simulator: a pencil or the tin has left the table (its centre past the table's edge or below its top). Real trial: the video shows a pencil or the tin falling off the table; putting it back does not restore the score. No penalty for which arm does what, for touching or moving the tin (the eleven are judged against the base wherever it lies), or for raising other pencils that end back in the base.
reset_notes: Lay the twelve pencils back in the base in the listed order, points to the left end, and slide them so the points are 4 to 5 mm from that end wall. Put the tin back on its marks with the lid open flat on the far side, and clear the pad. New pencils are factory-sharpened; if a point has been broken or resharpened to a different cone, replace that pencil. Prepare the modeled 1.2 mm flat at the point away from the robot, preserving the 11 mm cone, and remove all debris before placing the pencil in the tin. Use clean replaceable fingertip pads; inspect them and the pencils between trials, and replace damaged or shedding pencils.
fidelity: Rigid parts; contact and friction only, nothing scripted. Tin: maker's 186 x 102 x 12 mm and 157 g; base size, wall heights and sheet are estimates; lid rigid, open flat. Pencils: 7.5 x 176 mm, 11 mm cone, 5.5 g are estimates from the maker's photo; round barrels as 20-sided prisms; leads do not break. Friction estimates: pencil on tin 0.375, on fingertip 0.55, on pad 0.7. The pad is fixed. The demo video adds a close view from a spare camera; policy cameras, physics and scorer unchanged.
